section.title: Righteousness Through Faith
section.sectionRationale: This is the mountain peak of the letter and of the gospel itself. After proving the whole world guilty, Paul turns with two of the sweetest words in Scripture: but now. A righteousness of God apart from the law has been revealed, witnessed by the Law and the Prophets, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. Guilty sinners are justified freely by His grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation in His blood. In the cross God shows Himself to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Boasting is excluded, and the God of Jew and Gentile alike justifies by faith.
section.thesis: Because no one can be justified by works of the law, God has provided His own righteousness as a free gift, received by faith in Jesus Christ, grounded in the redemption and propitiating death of Christ, so that God is shown to be both perfectly just and the justifier of every believing sinner, Jew or Gentile, and all human boasting is forever excluded.
section.frameNote: Three movements: but now the righteousness of God revealed, given by faith to all who believe and justifying freely by grace; the cross as the propitiation that shows God to be just and the justifier; and the exclusion of boasting, with the one God justifying Jew and Gentile by faith while upholding the law.

units.label: But now the righteousness of God revealed
units.note: justified freely by grace, received by faith

verses.text: But now, apart from the law, the {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets.
And this righteousness from God comes through {{pistis|faith}} in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction,
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
and are justified freely by His {{charis|grace}} through the {{apolytrosis|redemption}} that is in Christ Jesus.

units.label: God set Him forth as a propitiation
units.note: the cross shows God just and the justifier

verses.text: God presented Him as an {{hilasterion|atoning sacrifice}} in His blood through faith, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand.
He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.

units.label: Boasting excluded, God of Jew and Gentile alike
units.note: justified by faith, yet the law upheld

verses.text: Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith.
For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too,
since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.
Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, a right standing before God and the saving activity of God that provides it. This righteousness is of God, from Him as gift and source, revealed apart from the law and yet witnessed by it. It is not a righteousness we produce but one God grants, credited to the believer through faith in Christ, the heart of the doctrine of justification.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, the empty hand that receives what God gives. Righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. Faith is not a work that earns; it is the means by which the sinner rests wholly on Christ and receives God's gift. Paul repeats it to exclude all boasting: the ground is Christ, the instrument is faith.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unearned favor toward the undeserving. Sinners are justified freely by His grace, a gift with no price attached and no merit required. Grace is the fountain of justification; because salvation is by grace it can only be received by faith, and boasting is forever shut out.

apolytrosis.gloss: Redemption, release secured by the payment of a ransom, as of a slave set free. Justification is free to us but costly to God, grounded in the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. The price was His own blood; the gift comes to us without charge because the ransom has already been paid in full.

hilasterion.gloss: Propitiation, the atoning sacrifice that turns away wrath, the word used for the mercy seat where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. God set forth Christ as the true mercy seat, bearing in His blood the wrath our sins deserved, so that God can be both just, not overlooking sin, and the justifier of all who trust in Jesus.

basic.context: Chapters 1 to 3 have driven relentlessly to one verdict: the whole world is guilty and no one can be justified by works of the law. Now, at the darkest point, Paul turns with but now. Everything changes. God Himself has provided the righteousness that no sinner could achieve, revealed in the gospel and grounded in the death of Jesus. This is the answer the letter has been building toward.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these verses slowly; every word is loaded. Righteousness of God, faith, grace, redemption, propitiation, justify, blood. Verses 21 to 26 form one of the densest and most important paragraphs in the Bible, often called the heart of Romans. The but now signals a decisive turn in the history of salvation: the promised righteousness has appeared. Verses 27 to 31 draw out the consequences, especially that boasting is excluded and the gospel is for Jew and Gentile alike.
basic.originalLanguages: The dikaiosyne, the righteousness of God, comes through pistis, faith, and is given by charis, grace. It rests on the apolytrosis, the redemption, the ransom paid in Christ, and on the hilasterion, the propitiation, Christ set forth as the atoning sacrifice in His blood. These words together carry the doctrine of justification: a gift, received by faith, purchased at the cross.
basic.typology: The hilasterion is the mercy seat of the ark, where atoning blood was sprinkled once a year; Christ is the true mercy seat, the place where God and sinners meet in mercy. The redemption echoes the exodus, God buying a people out of slavery, now fulfilled as Christ ransoms us from sin. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to this very righteousness.
basic.christ: Christ is everything here. He is the object of saving faith, the one in whom redemption is found, and the propitiation God set forth in His blood. At the cross He bore the wrath our sins deserved, so that God could remain just while justifying the guilty. The whole gospel narrows to a single scene: Jesus, the crucified mercy seat, in whom God is both the just Judge and the justifier of everyone who believes.
basic.god: God is the source, the actor, and the vindicated one in this passage. He reveals His righteousness, He justifies freely by His grace, He sets forth His Son as the propitiation, and He does it to demonstrate His own justice. The cross is not only love for sinners but the vindication of God's holiness: He does not sweep sin under the rug but deals with it fully, so as to be both just and the justifier.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 16 describes the mercy seat and the Day of Atonement behind the word propitiation. Habakkuk 2:4, the righteous will live by faith, is the letter's thesis. Ephesians 2:8-9 restates that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so no one may boast. Genesis 15:6, Abraham believed God and it was credited as righteousness, grounds justification by faith in the very Law that testifies to it.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible had promised that God would put things right and provide a righteousness His people could not earn. Sacrifices, the mercy seat, and the exodus all pointed forward. Here the promise arrives: but now the righteousness of God is revealed in Christ crucified, the true propitiation and redemption. The long story of a holy God saving guilty sinners without compromising His justice reaches its climax at the cross, thrown open to Jew and Gentile alike.

context.literary:
Romans 3:21-31 stands at the hinge of the letter. Everything from 1:18 to 3:20 has been a single indictment, and it ends with a shut mouth and a silent world, 3:19. Then comes the two small words that turn the book, nuni de, 'but now.' They are temporal and logical at once: a new moment in history has arrived, and a new answer to the charge has been given. The paragraph is also a deliberate echo of 1:16-17. There Paul promised that the gospel reveals the righteousness of God; here, at last, he shows how that righteousness can be given to people the earlier chapters have condemned.

Verses 21 to 26 are one long, tightly packed unit, and in the Greek they read almost as a single breath. Notice how the same ideas return from different angles. The righteousness of God is mentioned in verses 21, 22, 25 and 26, and each time a different side of it shows. In 21 it is attested by Scripture, in 22 it is received by faith, in 25 it is demonstrated at the cross, and in 26 it is vindicated, for God remains just. Verse 23 is the dark pivot in the middle of the bright sentence, and verse 24 begins with the participle 'being justified,' so that the whole gift hangs on the sinners it has just described.

Verses 27 to 31 shift into the diatribe style Paul has used since chapter 2, a dialogue with an imagined objector, built from rapid questions and short answers. Where is boasting? Excluded. Is God the God of Jews only? No. Do we nullify the law? Certainly not. The paragraph closes by taking up the very objection that will carry the next two chapters, namely whether faith overthrows the law, and the answer is promised in chapter 4: Abraham, the law's own witness, was justified by faith.
context.historical:
Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, most likely in the winter of AD 56 to 57, and was about to carry the collection to Jerusalem before turning west, Romans 15:25-29. The Roman church had been shaped by turbulence. Acts 18:2 records that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, and many think Jewish Christians began returning after his death, to find a church now largely Gentile. That is the setting for the question that haunts these verses: on what basis do two peoples with two histories share one table?

The vocabulary of verses 24 and 25 would have sounded very Jewish to the first hearers. Redemption language belonged to the exodus, where the LORD said He would redeem Israel with an outstretched arm, Exodus 6:6. The word translated 'atoning sacrifice,' hilasterion, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat, the golden cover of the ark where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year, Leviticus 16:14-15. By Paul's day the ark had long been gone from the temple, and the inner room stood empty. Paul announces that the place where God meets sinners in mercy is no longer a lid in a hidden room but a person set forth 'publicly' in history.

The phrase about God passing over sins 'committed beforehand,' verse 25, also had a background. The long patience of God toward the nations and toward Israel, Romans 2:4 and Acts 17:30, left a standing question: had God simply let sin go unanswered? Faithful Jews knew that sacrifices year after year could not finally settle the account, a point Hebrews 10:1-4 makes. Paul answers that God had been waiting for the day He would publicly settle it.
context.canonical:
The paragraph gathers threads from every part of the Old Testament. The Law and the Prophets 'attest' the righteousness of God, verse 21, and Paul has already cited witnesses from each: Habakkuk 2:4 for the prophets, and in the next chapter Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32:1-2 for the Law and the Writings. The psalmists had also sung of a righteousness that God reveals to the nations, Psalm 98:2, and confessed that no one alive is righteous before Him, Psalm 143:2, the very verse Paul echoes in Romans 3:20. Isaiah had promised that God's Servant would 'justify many' by bearing their iniquities, Isaiah 53:11, which is the doctrine of this paragraph in a single sentence from seven centuries earlier.

The Old Testament sacrificial pictures are fulfilled here. The mercy seat of Exodus 25:17-22 and the blood of Leviticus 16 meet in the one whom God 'set forth.' Hebrews 9:5 still names the mercy seat by the same Greek word, while Hebrews 9 and 10 unfold how Christ's blood did what the old blood could only point toward.

The rest of the New Testament repeats this paragraph in many voices. Galatians 2:16 states that no one is justified by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ, and Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is a gift of God, not from works, so that no one can boast. Acts 13:38-39 gives Paul's own sermon form of it. Second Corinthians 5:21 says how the exchange works, and 1 John 2:2 uses the same hilasterion family for Christ, the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to settle a question of rights and relationships as much as of salvation. He wants the believers in Rome, Jew and Gentile, to know that they have exactly the same footing before God, and that nothing in them, not heritage, not ritual, not moral effort, is part of the foundation. The aim is not only that individual sinners be forgiven, but that a divided congregation stop competing with itself. If every member has been justified by the same grace through the same faith, then boasting is gone and the walls between them have lost their ground.

He also intends to defend God. A reader who has just heard that God forgives guilty sinners may ask whether God has quietly lowered His standards. Paul's insistence, repeated in verses 25 and 26, that the cross demonstrates God's righteousness answers that charge. God is not careless about sin, and He does not forgive by pretending. He forgives at the cost of His own Son, and so He is seen to be both just and the one who justifies.

Finally Paul means the paragraph to protect the law as well as grace. Verse 31 refuses the idea that faith cancels Scripture. The law's testimony, its verdict on the world, its sacrifices and its promises, is upheld by the gospel because every strand of it finds its meaning in Christ.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this paragraph describes what God has done: He has revealed His righteousness, justified sinners freely, redeemed them, and set Christ forth as the atoning sacrifice. Nothing here is a command to be obeyed in the usual sense. It is a report of finished work, and the proper response is to receive it, not to add to it. That is why Paul can say the principle of boasting is the principle of faith, not works.

Some application does follow. If justification rests on grace alone, then neither pride nor despair has any footing. A believer who thinks his record makes him acceptable is boasting where Paul has silenced boasting, and a believer who thinks his failures have cancelled his acceptance is doubting the work of Christ, not his own. There is a social application as well. Because there is 'no distinction,' verse 22, churches should not set up spiritual classes by ethnicity, background or religious attainment. And because the law is upheld, believers are not freed from the moral shape of Scripture, only from the false hope of being saved by it. Paul takes up that second point at length in chapters 6 to 8.

debates.question: Does 'through faith in Jesus Christ' mean our faith in Him, or His own faithfulness?

views.label: Faith in Christ, the objective reading
views.case: The Greek of verse 22, pisteos Iesou Christou, literally 'faith of Jesus Christ,' can be read either way. The traditional reading takes it as faith directed at Christ. Paul adds 'to all who believe' in the same verse, and in verse 26 he speaks of the one who has faith in Jesus. Galatians 2:16 says that we 'have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ,' which would be oddly repetitive if the genitive meant His faithfulness.

views.label: The faithfulness of Christ, the subjective reading
views.case: Others point out that Paul elsewhere uses the plain Greek preposition for 'in' when he wants it, and that Romans 5:19 stresses the obedience of the one man. On this view the phrase names Christ's faithful obedience to the point of the cross as the ground of salvation, with the believer's faith appearing separately in 'to all who believe.' The sentence then is not redundant but complete: faithfulness of Christ, faith of the believer.

views.label: Both are true even if only one is meant here
views.case: A third group notes that the choice is less stark than it sounds. No one in the debate denies that Christ's obedience saves or that sinners must trust Him. They differ over what these particular words say.

debates.bearing: The grammar cannot settle this alone, and the surrounding verses carry the weight either way: the gift is grounded wholly in what Christ has done, and it is received by trust, with no contribution from the sinner.

debates.question: Is the hilasterion of verse 25 a sacrifice that removes guilt, or one that turns away God's wrath?

views.label: Propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away wrath
views.case: The word group in this setting carries the idea of averting anger. Paul has built the case on the wrath of God, 1:18 and 2:5, and in 5:9 he says believers are saved from that wrath through Christ's blood. Verses 25 and 26 also speak of God demonstrating His righteousness, which suggests that the cross answers a real divine judgment, not only a human problem. This is the historic Protestant reading, and the BSB footnote offers 'propitiation' as an alternative translation.

views.label: Expiation, a sacrifice that cleanses sin
views.case: Some argue that in the Greek Old Testament God is the one who provides the covering and never needs to be appeased from outside, so that the focus falls on removing sin and its defilement, as Leviticus 16:16 speaks of cleansing the Most Holy Place. They say the translation 'atoning sacrifice' captures that fully.

views.label: The mercy seat itself
views.case: A third view stresses that the Greek word is the one used for the mercy seat, Exodus 25:17-22 and Hebrews 9:5, so that Paul calls Christ the place where God meets sinners. On this reading the word names the setting of atonement more than the mechanism.

debates.bearing: The views are not mutually exclusive. Scripture shows God Himself providing the sacrifice, so wrath is not appeased by an outside party, and the same cross both removes sin and satisfies His justice. Verses 25 and 26, with their stress on the demonstration of righteousness, make the wrath-bearing dimension hard to leave out.

debates.question: What is the 'righteousness of God' that is revealed?

views.label: A status given to the believer
views.case: The Reformers read the phrase as a righteousness that comes from God and is credited to those who believe. Verse 22 says it is 'from God' and 'to all who believe,' and Philippians 3:9 speaks of 'the righteousness from God on the basis of faith.'

views.label: God's own faithfulness to His covenant
views.case: Others stress that in the Old Testament the righteousness of God is often His saving faithfulness, Psalm 98:2, and that Paul links it to God proving Himself right, Romans 3:4 and 3:25-26. So the phrase names God's own action as much as a gift.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many hold that Paul's usage joins the two. The same saving act in which God is shown to be righteous is the act that makes sinners righteous.

debates.bearing: Verse 26 holds the two together by saying God is 'just and the one who justifies.' His own righteousness is displayed in the act that gives a righteous standing to believers.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb 'justify,' dikaioo, which governs the paragraph, 3:24, 26 and 28. It is a legal word, the opposite of 'condemn,' and the Old Testament uses it for a judge declaring someone in the right. Proverbs 17:15 calls it an abomination to acquit the guilty, and Exodus 23:7 has God say He will not acquit the guilty. Paul's claim is bold for exactly this reason. God does what He forbids a human judge to do, and He does it without becoming unjust, which is the whole burden of verses 25 and 26.

Verse 23 holds a small grammar lesson. 'All have sinned' is in the aorist, which looks at the sum of human failure as a single act, and 'fall short' is in the present tense, a continuing condition. Humanity both did sin and keeps missing. Many take the 'glory of God' they miss to be the image-bearing destiny of Genesis 1:26, the radiance that was meant to belong to humanity.

In verse 24 'freely' is dorean, built on the word for a gift, dorea, and it means that the justification costs the receiver nothing, a point Paul uses again in 5:15 and 5:17. 'Redemption,' apolytrosis, comes from lytron, a ransom price, the word used in Mark 10:45 for the life given for many. The picture is of a captive set free by a payment.

Verse 25 begins with proetheto, 'set forth,' a verb that can mean to display publicly or to purpose beforehand. Both fit: God planned it and showed it openly. The word for 'forbearance' is anoche, the same word as in 2:4, the patience of God holding back judgment. 'Passed over,' paresis, is not the same as forgiveness, aphesis, the word in Acts 13:38. Paresis describes a deferral of the penalty, a debt left unpaid for the moment, and the cross is the day the debt is paid. Paul calls it an endeixis, a demonstration or public proof, and the word appears in both verse 25 and verse 26.

Verse 21 says the righteousness is 'attested,' martyroumene, a present participle from the word for witness. The Law and the Prophets keep on giving testimony, as in a court. Verse 27 asks about the 'principle,' nomos, of boasting, using the word for law in a looser sense: a governing rule or way of operating. Verse 31 closes with the verb histemi, 'we uphold' or 'we establish,' the opposite of nullify. The law is not demolished but given the foundation it never had under works.

Finally, verse 30 has 'since there is only one God,' which echoes the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4. Paul uses Israel's most basic creed to prove that God must treat Jew and Gentile alike. If the LORD is One, He cannot keep two ways of salvation. Both groups are justified by faith, and the Greek uses two prepositions, ek pisteos for the circumcised and dia tes pisteos for the uncircumcised, but the same faith stands behind both.

typology.fulfillment: The mercy seat was the golden cover of the ark, where God said He would meet Israel, and where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year, Leviticus 16:14-15. Paul uses its Greek name for Christ, and Hebrews 9:5 shows the title was familiar. The escalation is from a lid in a curtained room, approached by one man on one day, to a person set forth in the open for everyone who believes. It falls short as a type because the old blood had to be brought again each year, Hebrews 10:1-4, while this blood is shed once and never repeated.

The exodus was Israel's great story of redemption, a people bought out of slavery with an outstretched arm. 'Redemption' in verse 24 pulls that history into the gospel. In Christ the payment is not bricks and tribute but His blood, and the captivity is not Egypt but sin and death. Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type falls short because Israel was freed from a human master and still carried a hard heart, while the redemption in Christ reaches the heart.

On one day each year the high priest entered the Most Holy Place with blood for himself and the people. The language of passing over sins in verse 25 recalls how each year's sacrifice held the account open until the next. Christ completes the ritual by entering once, Hebrews 9:11-12, with His own blood, so that the account is closed. The type falls short because the high priest was a sinner needing atonement for himself, and Christ is both priest and offering, without sin.

typology.type: The Servant who justifies many, Isaiah 53:11
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah describes a righteous Servant who justifies many by bearing their iniquities, and the language of justification there is the very language of Romans 3. The pattern of one righteous person counted on behalf of many is fulfilled in Jesus, who was made sin so that others might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Here the correspondence is exact, the Servant and the sinner exchange places, but it also goes beyond what Isaiah could see, since the many include Gentiles from every nation.

study.christ:
Everything in this paragraph is Christ, but it helps to see the several ways the text points to Him. First, He is the location of redemption: it is 'in Christ Jesus,' verse 24. Paul does not say the price was paid somewhere out of sight and then applied. The redemption is in a person, and the believer receives it by being joined to Him, a theme that bursts out in chapters 6 to 8.

Second, He is the public display of God's righteousness. Verse 25 says God set Him forth, a word that suggests an open exhibition, and the story of the gospels bears that out: Jesus was lifted up in a place where the whole world's powers, Rome, the priesthood, the crowd, could see what was done. John 12:32 records Jesus saying that when He was lifted up He would draw all people to Himself. The cross is where the unseen righteousness of God becomes visible.

Third, He is the one in whom justice and mercy meet without contradiction. Verse 26 says God did this to be 'just and the one who justifies.' Romans 8:3 says God condemned sin in the flesh of His own Son, and 2 Corinthians 5:21 says the sinless one was made sin on our behalf so that we might become the righteousness of God. The language is of an exchange, not an illusion: the guilt is dealt with in the one who bears it, and the standing is given to the ones who receive it. This answers the charge that God has merely looked the other way.

Fourth, He is the fulfillment of what the Law and the Prophets attested. Paul can say the righteousness is attested by them because the shape of Jesus' death is already visible in the mercy seat, the Passover lamb, the Servant of Isaiah 53 and the promise to Abraham. Jesus Himself said that the Scriptures bear witness about Him, John 5:39, and on the Emmaus road He opened the Law and the Prophets to show that the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory, Luke 24:25-27.

Fifth, He is the object of faith. Paul never says that faith justifies as a work or a quality. Faith is the empty hand that takes what Christ has finished. That is why Acts 13:39 says everyone who believes is justified through Him from everything the law could not clear.

A caution applies. The typology here is real but should not be pressed into details the text does not give, such as the colour of the blood or the dimensions of the mercy seat. The link rests on clear texts: the mercy seat title, the Day of Atonement background, and the explicit statements of the New Testament.
study.god:
This paragraph shows God at His most unified. The same God is just and merciful, holy and gracious, and the whole point of verses 25 and 26 is that He is not forced to choose between them. Many religions picture a deity who must either enforce the rules and condemn, or relax them and forgive. Paul says God does neither of those things. He keeps His justice perfectly and extends mercy fully, and He does it through His own act.

God is also the initiator in every verb. He reveals His righteousness, verse 21. He justifies, verse 24. He presents Christ, verse 25. He passed over sins in His forbearance. The believer's part is expressed only in the passive and the receptive: 'being justified,' 'through faith.' The doctrine of grace is not a theory about human effort being insufficient; it is a portrait of a God who does the whole work.

His patience is another attribute on show. 'Forbearance' in verse 25 recalls the kindness, tolerance and patience of 2:4. God held back judgment for ages, and verse 26 says He did so with an end in view. His patience is not indifference or weakness; it is the long preparation of a moment when righteousness and mercy would meet. Second Peter 3:9 says the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise but patient with us.

The paragraph also shows God's impartiality and oneness. Verse 29 asks whether God is the God of the Jews only, and the answer rests on God's being One, Deuteronomy 6:4. A single Creator who made all peoples cannot be a tribal deity. His justifying work is therefore universal in reach, 'to all who believe,' and personal in application, 'the one who has faith in Jesus.'

For worship, this means that the proper response to this passage is not self-congratulation but adoration. Boasting is excluded, verse 27, but praise is not. Paul's doxology comes shortly in 11:33-36, and the shape of it is already here: since nothing in us contributed to the gift, all the glory belongs to God. The paragraph also steadies the conscience. A believer who wonders whether God is secretly angry or whether his record might still undo him can look at verse 26, where God has staked His own righteousness on justifying everyone who trusts Jesus. He cannot cancel the verdict without denying Himself.

crossReferences.note: The high priest sprinkles the blood on and before the mercy seat so that atonement is made for the Most Holy Place and the people. The ritual lies behind the hilasterion of verse 25 and shows what kind of thing Paul calls Christ: the place where blood is offered and God meets sinners.

God promises to meet Israel above the mercy seat between the cherubim. The golden lid, set over the Testimony, shows that mercy covered the law that condemned. Paul's use of the same Greek word tells readers that Christ is now that meeting place.

The righteous will live by faith, set against the proud one who is not upright. Paul cites it in Romans 1:17 as the theme of the letter, and 3:22 to 28 unpacks it, so that faith is not a rival to righteousness but the way it is received.

No one alive is righteous before God, and the psalmist begs not to be brought into judgment. Paul echoes it in 3:20 and it gives the other half of the paragraph: if no one can stand on his own record, the only hope is a righteousness that comes from outside.

The righteous Servant will justify many and bear their iniquities. Here the same pair of ideas, justification and bearing sin, occurs in one verse, and Paul's exposition of the cross in verses 24 to 26 reads like a commentary on it.

The theme of the letter, stated before the long case against humanity. The gospel reveals the righteousness of God from faith to faith. Romans 3:21 returns to the same phrase after the verdict of guilt, as if to say the promise made in chapter 1 has now been explained.

Paul says that those who are now justified by His blood will be saved from wrath through Him. It shows what the blood of verse 25 accomplishes, and it connects justification to final salvation, so that the present verdict carries a future guarantee.

Paul's shortest statement of the same doctrine, with a threefold repetition that no one is justified by works of the law. It was written in the middle of a dispute over Jew and Gentile at table, and it shows the concrete shape of boasting that verse 27 excludes.

God made the sinless one to be sin on our behalf so that we might become the righteousness of God. It tells how the demonstration of verse 26 works as an exchange: our sin lies on Christ, and His standing is given to us.

Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch compresses the gospel into forgiveness through Jesus and justification for everyone who believes from what the law of Moses could not clear. It shows that Romans 3 was not new teaching but the heart of his preaching from the start.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first question after Genesis 3 is whether a holy God can live with sinners, and every sacrifice, altar and tabernacle that follows is a partial answer. Abel's offering, Noah's altar, the Passover lamb and the blood on the mercy seat all keep the question open in the most urgent way, because each one covered sin without ending it. Habakkuk's prophecy that the righteous will live by faith, Isaiah's Servant who bears iniquity, and the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:34, that God will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more, sharpen the question into a longing.

Romans 3:21 is where the longing is answered. The 'but now' marks a point in history, not only in an argument: the age of promise, patience and shadow gives way to the age of the revealed righteousness. The cross is the moment when what God has been holding in reserve is made public, and the sins He passed over are finally dealt with.

What follows from this paragraph is the rest of the story. Because God is the justifier, His people are no longer defined by ancestry or ritual but by faith, and so the family of Abraham opens to the nations, as the next chapter will show. Because the guilty are justified, they can be brought into peace with God, Romans 5:1, and into a new life by the Spirit, Romans 8. Because the verdict is already given, the final judgment holds no terror for those in Christ, Romans 8:1.

The story ends where this paragraph points. In Revelation the redeemed stand before the throne in robes washed in the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 7:14, and the one on the throne declares that God Himself will dwell with them, Revelation 21:3. The righteousness revealed in Romans 3 is the only reason that scene is possible. The mercy seat has become a throne, and the ones who once fell short of the glory of God share in it.

quiz.q: What decisive turn does Paul announce with the words but now in verse 21?

options.text: A righteousness of God, apart from the law, has been revealed and attested by the Law and the Prophets.
options.note: Verse 21 exactly: the righteousness of God is now revealed apart from the law, witnessed by Scripture.

options.text: God has unveiled His own saving righteousness quite apart from law keeping.
options.note: Right in substance, though it omits that the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it.

options.text: God has finally made the law easier for people to keep.
options.note: The righteousness comes apart from the law, not by making law keeping easier.

options.text: God has abandoned righteousness as a requirement altogether.
options.note: The opposite; God reveals and upholds His righteousness while giving it as a gift.

quiz.q: On what basis are guilty sinners justified, according to verse 24?

options.text: Freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
options.note: Verse 24 states it word for word: justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ.

options.text: As a free gift of God's favor, grounded in Christ's redeeming work.
options.note: Accurate in meaning; the text names grace as the source and redemption in Christ as the ground.

options.text: By a combination of God's grace and their own sincere efforts.
options.note: Paul says freely by grace; adding human effort contradicts the gift and reintroduces boasting.

options.text: By strictly keeping the works of the law.
options.note: Paul has just said no one is justified by works of the law; justification is by grace.

quiz.q: What does it mean that God set Christ forth as a propitiation in His blood (verses 25 to 26)?

options.text: Christ bore in His blood the wrath our sins deserved, so God is both just and the justifier.
options.note: The propitiation turns away wrath, letting God remain just while justifying believers.

options.text: At the cross God dealt fully with sin so He could forgive without compromising His justice.
options.note: Correct in substance; the fuller answer names the wrath-bearing propitiation in Christ's blood.

options.text: God simply overlooked sin out of kindness without any atoning sacrifice.
options.note: The passage says the opposite; God demonstrates His righteousness rather than overlooking sin.

options.text: Christ set a moral example that inspires people to reform themselves.
options.note: The cross is a propitiation in His blood, not merely an inspiring example.

quiz.q: Why is human boasting excluded (verses 27 to 28)?

options.text: Because a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, so no one contributes merit.
options.note: Verses 27 and 28: boasting is excluded on the principle of faith, not works.

options.text: Because salvation is received by faith, not achieved by our own doing.
options.note: Right in meaning; Paul specifies justification by faith apart from works of the law.

options.text: Because only a few especially holy people are allowed to boast.
options.note: Paul excludes all boasting, not merely most of it; the ground is faith, not attainment.

options.text: Because good works count for nothing in the Christian life ever.
options.note: Paul excludes boasting in works as the ground of justification, not the value of good works as fruit.

quiz.q: How does Paul answer whether justification by faith nullifies the law (verse 31)?

options.text: Certainly not; instead, we uphold the law.
options.note: Verse 31 exactly: faith does not nullify but upholds the law.

options.text: No; this faith actually establishes and confirms the law rather than cancelling it.
options.note: Correct in meaning; Paul says we uphold the law, not overthrow it.

options.text: Yes; faith makes the law completely irrelevant and void.
options.note: Paul says certainly not; faith upholds the law rather than voiding it.

options.text: The question does not matter, since the law was never from God.
options.note: Paul honors the law as God's; he affirms that faith upholds it.

questions: Paul turns the whole argument with but now. How does it strike you that the announcement of grace comes precisely at the point where every mouth is stopped and no one can save himself?
Righteousness comes freely by grace through faith, not by works. Where are you still tempted to add your own performance to Christ's finished work as the ground of your acceptance?
At the cross God is shown to be both just and the justifier. Why does it matter for your assurance that God did not merely overlook your sin but dealt with it fully in Christ?
The word propitiation means Christ bore the wrath your sin deserved. How does dwelling on the cost of your redemption deepen your love and worship?
Boasting is excluded, and God justifies Jew and Gentile the same way. How should being saved entirely by grace shape your humility toward God and your welcome of others who trust in Christ?
Paul insists that faith upholds rather than nullifies the law. How does being justified by faith free you to love God's commands rather than fear them?

translationNotes.note: Through faith in Jesus Christ can be read as the believer's faith in Christ, the historic and contextual reading, or as the faithfulness of Christ. The surrounding phrases, to all who believe and the one who has faith in Jesus, favor faith as the sinner's trust; either way salvation rests wholly on Christ.

The word rendered atoning sacrifice is hilasterion, meaning propitiation, the turning away of wrath, and also the term for the mercy seat of the ark. The BSB footnote itself offers or as a propitiation. Christ is both the wrath-bearer and the true mercy seat where God meets sinners in mercy.

Justified by faith apart from works of the law is the sentence at the heart of the Reformation. Works of the law are deeds of obedience to the Mosaic law; Paul denies they justify, insisting acceptance with God is by faith alone in Christ.
